库克现身广州，探班 iPhone 18 Pro 咏春短片拍摄现场
10 月 10 日，苹果董事会执行主席蒂姆·库克（Tim Cook）再次来到中国，并将此行首站选在广州，探班使用 iPhone 18 Pro 系列拍摄的咏春主题短片。
拍摄由青年导演古天鸡与咏春拳传承人戴子龙参与，在岭南风格的园林实景中，通过手机影像呈现中国传统武术。
探班期间，库克现场观看了咏春拳演示，并与主创团队交流移动影像拍摄及专业工作流程。据介绍，拍摄团队利用 iPhone 18 Pro 系列的摄像头系统，在低光环境下记录快速变化的咏春招式。此外，古天鸡团队还向库克展示了一份使用 iPad Pro 搭配 Apple Pencil Pro 绘制的「武功秘籍」，以数字绘画的形式呈现咏春拳法。
库克随后在社交平台表示：「很高兴再次来到中国！在广州第一次透过 iPhone 18 Pro 镜头感受咏春的魅力，真是一次难忘的体验。」
值得一提的是，这是库克今年 9 月卸任苹果 CEO、转任董事会执行主席后首次到访中国。苹果现任 CEO 为约翰·特努斯（John Ternus）。
曝苹果 iPhone Duo 加单 30%，Pro 系列总订单量不变
据证券时报报道，苹果对今年秋季新款手机的订单作出结构性调整：iPhone Duo 加单 30%，调整后的总量仍未超过 1000 万台。
与此同时，iPhone 18 Pro 订单减少 10% 至 15%，iPhone 18 Pro Max 订单增加 10% 至 15%，Pro 系列总订单量保持不变。报道援引苹果供应链人士称，订单结构正向价值更高的产品倾斜，预计有利于相关供应链公司的业绩。
苹果第二期中国清洁能源基金扩容至 2.12 亿美元
10 月 10 日，苹果宣布第二期中国清洁能源基金的承诺投资总额增至 2.12 亿美元，约合 14 亿元人民币。新能源科技、鹏鼎控股与达尔科技等供应商加入出资，基金已完成初步投资，支持广西 260 兆瓦、山东 50 兆瓦两处风电项目，均已开工建设。
苹果同时公布，其在中国超过 95% 的直接生产制造现已采用可再生能源，目标是到 2030 年底在全球供应链全面使用可再生能源。由施罗德资本管理的第二期基金，计划每年为中国电网新增 110 万兆瓦时的风能和太阳能发电能力。
在工业供热减排方面，苹果正与山东创新精密推进铝材熔炼电气化，将已完成示范运行的电感应炉技术用于 MacBook Air 规模化生产。苹果还将向中国绿色碳汇基金会和北京自然之友公益基金会提供新资助，分别支持森林与城市碳汇试点、社区应对气候变化方案。
四部门拟禁全隐藏式车门把手，要求车企如实宣传使用边界
10 月 10 日，工业和信息化部等四部门发布汽车产品创新设计和研发测试验证管理通知征求意见稿，拟禁止配备全隐藏式门把手，并要求车企真实、客观开展营销宣传，如实说明创新设计的使用边界、限制条件和测试验证情况。
征求意见稿针对跟风推出新产品、测试验证不充分等问题提出要求：涉及安全的应急操纵件应保留实体操纵件和醒目标识；门把手须具备机械冗余设计和手部操作空间，并验证极端环境及紧急情况下的可操作性。行车时不可使用「零重力」座椅、旋转座椅或座椅放倒成床等功能。
按拟议安排，2027 年 1 月 1 日起，涉及创新设计的新申报产品需补充技术参数并完成相应测试；已取得公告的产品应在 2027 年 7 月 1 日前补报参数及验证材料。环境适应性验证周期不少于 1 年，可靠性验证试验不低于 3 万公里。
宣传方面，车企不得作虚假、夸大或引人误解的宣传，不得使用违反道路交通法规的场景展示产品功能，也不得诱导驾驶人忽视安全驾驶责任。上述要求目前处于公开征求意见阶段。
字节据报加速个人 AI 智能体，拟将 Spell 与豆包结合
据财新报道，字节跳动正在加快个人 AI 智能体的研发，计划把代号为 Spell 的项目与豆包产品结合，尽快对外推出。财新 10 月 9 日从字节内部人士处获悉，这项研发在国庆假期前已加紧推进。
Spell 项目于今年 4 月启动，延续了 2025 年豆包手机助手在个人智能体方向上的探索。彼时，豆包内部已启动相关产品内测。
报道介绍，新产品由豆包手机助手团队主导，Spell 项目与豆包对话团队共同负责。Meta Muse 等个人智能体在海外走红后，字节进一步加快了项目进度。
Meta 据报暂缓向 Anthropic 提供 AI 算力
据《华尔街日报》报道，Anthropic 首席执行官 Dario Amodei 今年早些时候曾致电 Meta 首席 AI 官 Alexandr Wang，寻求更多算力。Meta 内部讨论后，最终决定暂时不向 Anthropic 提供芯片算力。
Claude Code 的意外走红让 Anthropic 遭遇算力紧张，并导致服务频繁中断。为寻找资源，联合创始人 Tom Brown 在 3 月底到 xAI 办公室与马斯克商谈；Anthropic 随后于 5 月宣布与 SpaceX 达成协议，租用超过 300 兆瓦算力。
报道指出，大量数据中心仍处于建设阶段，眼下可实际使用的容量远少于宣布中的规模。成熟供应商开始要求多年合同和更高预付款，一些初创公司则转向安全或基础设施较弱的服务商。还有公司为防备未来短缺而超额预订，也有公司因产品需求不及预期，被迫转售剩余容量。
Netflix 称约 300 部作品已使用 AI，导演谈降本与创作取舍
Netflix 亚太制作高级总监 Lee Sung-gyun 在釜山国际电影节论坛上表示，公司约有 300 部作品已以不同方式使用 AI，应用环节包括预演、美术设计、布景构思、剪辑和视觉特效。
据 Variety 现场报道，Netflix 展示了旗下 Eyeline 工作室结合实拍、传统特效和生成工具的混合制作流程。印度作品《Glory》也借助 AI 与视觉特效完成大规模人群场面；Lee 称，在原有预算和工期下，这些镜头本来可能被舍弃。
同场的《犯罪都市》导演姜允成介绍，他为海上军事题材项目《The Gulf of Aden》用可灵制作过全 AI 测试片。团队为融资测算时，预计采用这套流程可将制作预算降低约 40%，节省来自特效、拍摄简化与周期缩短。这是具体项目的测算，并非已完成影片的普遍降本比例。
姜允成同时指出，AI 让一些曾因预算取消的项目重新具备可行性，但也可能省去多人讨论、尝试和积累经验的过程。他认为，画面质量虽提升，传达情感、打动观众仍需人的创作；Lee 也强调，生成结果最终需要人再处理一次。
长鑫披露 4F² 内存架构进展，首款服务器产品预计年底推出
长鑫存储总裁曹堪宇在 10 月 10 日的第四届集成芯片和芯粒大会上披露，长鑫预计年底推出采用 4F² 架构的新一代 DDR5 RDIMM 服务器内存产品。据第一财经、21 世纪经济报道，这项技术在存储单元和制造工艺两方面作出调整。
目前 DRAM 主流存储单元采用 6F² 架构，F 代表最小特征尺寸。4F² 将单元面积缩小至四倍最小特征尺寸的平方，提高单位面积的存储密度。长鑫采用自研 VSG 垂直包围沟道晶体管，让晶体管竖立布置，以增强栅极控制能力，改善漏电与短沟道效应。
另一项调整是将 DRAM 存储阵列与 CMOS 外围逻辑电路的制造工艺分开，再通过晶圆级混合键合实现互联，使逻辑性能和存储密度可以分别优化。曹堪宇称，长鑫相关公开专利族已超过 300 件。
首代产品选择服务器用 DDR5 RDIMM，这类内存需要满足持续运行、稳定性和兼容性要求。此次披露的是研发进展与年底产品计划。
英伟达据报洽谈收购 Reflection AI，也可能追加投资
据《金融时报》援引直接知情人士报道，英伟达正就收购美国开放权重模型公司 Reflection AI，或进一步加深投资关系展开谈判。磋商仍在早期，交易可能在未来数周达成，也可能告吹，双方均拒绝置评。
潜在方案包括完整收购、追加股权投资，以及「收购式招聘」：英伟达聘用其员工并获得技术许可。另一种可能是提供更多芯片和算力。《金融时报》称，英伟达已向 Reflection 投入 8 亿美元，是其最大股东之一；这家公司今年 3 月融资时的估值为 250 亿美元。
Reflection 由曾参与 Google Gemini 研发的 Misha Laskin 和 Ioannis Antonoglou 创立，本周刚推出首款可定制的公开 AI 产品，运行在英伟达芯片上。开放权重模型允许用户在自己的硬件上运行并进行定制，Reflection 也是美国发展本土开放模型生态的参与者。
英伟达已有 Nemotron 开放权重模型系列。《金融时报》指出，公司目前仍缺少自己的前沿规模模型。
东芝人力负责人：AI 改变初级岗位，面试更看重解决问题的过程
AI 开始筛选简历之后，初级招聘人员如何积累经验？东芝美洲区首席人力资源官 Jason Richard Desentz 在 Business Insider 刊发的口述文章中表示，初级岗位仍会保留，但工作内容和招聘标准正在变化。
他举例说，面对上千份简历，招聘人员往往看完前几十份、找到一些合适人选就会停下，余下的好候选人可能被漏掉。东芝为招聘建立 AI Bot，希望让人员把时间转向与经理确认需求、设计更好的问题和改善新人入职体验；AI 生成的面试指南也应帮助找到需要追问的地方，而非直接排除可能学会工作的人。
面试时，Desentz 更关注候选人如何拆解问题、用数据支持判断、推动没有积极参与的同组成员，以及面对突然变化的预算或任务期限如何调整方案。没有工作经验的人，也可以用大学里的真实经历说明思考过程。
对于员工担忧，他主张承认工作正在变化，带着团队一起应对。东芝从员工最不喜欢的重复事务入手试做 Bot，并安排 AI 基础课程和内部展示。他强调要给员工留出试验时间，允许他们在学习中犯错。
腾讯云开源 TeamAI，团队 Skill 可跨 Agent 共享
腾讯云近日对外介绍并开源内部使用的 TeamAI 工具，希望把分散在不同 AI 编程工具里的团队配置、Skill 和经验，通过 Git 仓库统一管理。项目采用 MIT 许可证，已提供 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor、CodeBuddy 等工具的适配。
TeamAI 将能力分为三层：
团队执行层：集中发布 Skill、Rules、MCP、文档和模型配置，让成员在不同 Agent 中使用同一套团队规范；支持在新会话中同步管理员发布的更新。
团队上下文层：汇集项目知识、任务经验和代码知识图谱，并以 teamwiki 等形式供后续任务使用。
团队改进层：通过使用情况、会话记录和看板观察团队采用情况，帮助维护共享配置。
后两层仍标记为 Beta。成员可以继续使用各自熟悉的编程工具，团队共享内容则在同一仓库内维护和更新。
银河战舰 700 上市，先享价 17.98 万元起

阿里 Qoder 上线 Fast 模式，首次响应缩短至 3 秒
阿里 Qoder 10 月 10 日上线 Fast 模式，率先用于桌面端，需更新至 0.4.4 及以上版本。个人版和企业版均可使用，中国版与国际版同步支持。
中国版新增 Fast 档位，国际版原有的 Performance 模式则直接升级为 Fast，原用户无需额外操作。官方给出的数据是，首次响应时间由 8 秒缩短至 3 秒，Credits 消耗系数由 1.1x 降至 0.8x，约减少 27%；其表示输出质量保持不变。

罗技预览矩阵式会议音箱，可将两种语言投向不同座区
罗技 10 月 8 日预览 Rally Speaker 2 Pro 和 Rally Speaker 2 Max 两款音频系统，以自研 Sound Shape 技术进入专业视听市场。两款音箱安装在房间前方，分别使用 32 个和 64 个微型驱动单元，面向大型会议室和培训空间。
这套系统通过控制声波的叠加与抵消，把声音投向指定听音区域，同时减少声音向墙壁等方向扩散。罗技称，这可以降低反射和回声，并让前后排保持更均匀的音量，减少传统天花板音箱的布线和安装需求。
罗技还演示了一个仍在开发的多语言方案：单台 Max 可同时把两路不同音频投向房间两侧，例如左侧听英语、右侧听法语。公司正与合作伙伴研究接入 Microsoft Teams 的 Interpreter 和 Zoom Meetings 的 Voice Translator。
两款产品现可在罗技硅谷体验中心演示，计划于 2027 年夏季商业上市。
RSIGym 开源，让 AI 自主设计实验、训练并改进模型
Evolvent AI 团队开源了 RSIGym，把训练、推理、评测和沙箱执行做成 AI 可以调用的服务。研究 Agent 自行设计实验、生成训练数据、训练候选模型，再根据结果调整方案；平台统一管理权限和预算，并公开实验轨迹。
环境提供三种路线：只改训练数据、固定模型权重而改执行框架，以及同时优化数据、训练设置和框架。主实验让 6 个研究 Agent 在 5 个领域中改进同一个起点：Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base 加最小执行框架，每次基准实验的平台服务预算为 500 美元，研究 Agent 推理和最终正式评测费用另计。
团队报告，30 次联合优化实验中有 29 次优于初始系统。Opus 5 的 RSI-Index 最高，为 0.4809，表示平均弥补了距满分剩余差距的 48.09%，并非最终准确率。每种研究配置只运行一次，最终评测复用了开发阶段可见的任务。
另一项让 Qwen3.8-27B 研究自身的实验，则从初始 56.66% 降至 56.26%：小规模开发集上的进步没有转化为整体提升。该结果展示了自动研究的可执行过程，也保留了自我改进未必奏效的边界。
2027 款启源 A06 上市，限时权益价 11.69 万元起

lululemon 开启「一起好状态」活动，会发声的乒乓台来到上海
lululemon 连续第六年发起「一起好状态」年度活动。10 月 7 日，首场感受日在上海上音歌剧院举行，李宇春、邓亚萍、残奥铁三运动员王家超、人文学者梁永安及正念导师 Jesse Israel，通过演讲、对话和呼吸习练，讨论身体、心理与社交三个维度的好状态。
艺术家 James de Wulf 创作的「幸福的回响」乒乓台也首次来到中国。这件曾在 2025 年巴黎 Design Miami 展出的装置，以经过特殊调音的哑光铝板制作，乒乓球落在不同位置时会触发不同音调。邓亚萍与艺术家在现场挥拍演示了这套声音互动。
10 月 8 日至 18 日，乒乓台将在上海西岸中环限时展出，公众可参与体验。10 月 10 日至 17 日，lululemon 还将联合上海多家场馆推出八天主题热汗课程，全国门店同步举办系列课程。活动将上音歌剧院的对话与运动体验延伸至社区。
七部门发文纠治电商「自动跟价」「全网最低价」竞争
商务部等七部门发布实施品质电商「五优」行动的通知，提出协同整治无序非理性竞争，纠治电商平台「自动跟价」「全网最低价」等行为，并规范平台佣金抽成、商家评级规则，避免挤压品质商家的生存空间。
通知要求，电商平台制定、修改规则时，落实规则公示和公开征求意见；优化商品展示、推荐和营销活动机制，将商品质量、服务口碑和信用信息作为品质导向。有关部门还将建立平台与中小商家的对话沟通机制，打击刷单炒信。
在全链路品控方面，通知引导平台建立首席质量官制度，完善线上服务质量评价体系，并支持政务数据核验，协助平台比对商家证照。围绕「618」「双 11」等消费节点，各方将加强对平台的指导与规范。
胖东来梦之城公示酒店规划，高度不超过 99.95 米

另外两个配套项目中，二期幸福讲堂面积 5630 平方米、高度不超过 24 米；三期文化中心面积约 3.62 万平方米、高度不超过 25.45 米。
据极目新闻此前披露的规划信息，梦之城一期主要建设商业综合体，建筑面积约 46.7 万平方米，主体共 8 层。项目位于许昌市东城区、莲城大道以北和许州路以东，临近高铁许昌东站。
于东来曾在 7 月表示，梦之城将在 3 年内开业。此次公示展示的是酒店等后续配套的规划内容。
是周末啊！
One Fun Thing｜经典 Fiat 500 变身电动海滨小车
意大利汽车定制工作室 Garage Italia 把经典 Fiat 500 Spiaggina 改造成了一辆电动敞篷小车。它沿用无车门、开放式车身与可拆卸顶篷的海滨车设定，面向停靠地中海港口后、需要在沿岸小镇短途出行的游艇用户。
据 Design Milk 介绍，这辆车在后部装入电动机，搭配 11kWh 电池，WLTP 续航约 140 公里。车主可以选择 18 种车身颜色，也可以定制色彩；顶篷、坐垫采用意大利纺织品牌 Mariaflora 的面料，Bonacina 手工编织的座椅则提供藤编或耐日晒、盐雾的复合材料版本，地板使用防水 EVA 材料。
这套改造保留了 Fiat 500 Jolly 当年为海边休闲出行而做的形态，动力改成电驱后，游艇上也无需再为它携带汽油。车辆起价为 8.5 万欧元，选装和税费另计。
周末看什么｜《Animals》让一场绑架案撕开竞选家庭的秘密
洛杉矶市长候选人 Mark Kimball 正在为选举奔忙，一通电话却告知他的儿子遭到绑架。在 Netflix 已上线的惊悚片《Animals》中，他与妻子 Abigail 必须筹措赎金，而夫妻关系、竞选利益与家庭秘密也在这一夜接连暴露。
影片由本·阿弗莱克执导并出演 Mark，凯丽·华盛顿饰演 Abigail，史蒂文·元饰演竞选经理，吉莲·安德森出演协助处理危机的神秘掮客。故事在洛杉矶展开，竞选团队试图维持的公众形象，与一家人在绑架案中的选择不断发生冲突。
Variety 影评人 Guy Lodge 肯定影片紧凑的推进和阿弗莱克逐渐失控的表演，也指出政治讽刺、婚姻冲突与通俗惊悚元素之间的切换，削弱了部分情节的真实感。他认为影片靠接连转折保持吸引力，但没有把对权力和不平等的追问展开到底。
买书不读指南｜《创意行为：存在即答案》从注意力谈起
音乐制作人里克·鲁宾在《创意行为：存在即答案》中，把创作放回日常的观察、感知和选择。他以自己与不同类型音乐人合作的经验为起点，讨论怎样留意线索、保存灵感、进行试验，以及把尚未成形的想法逐步推进到完成。
全书由 78 篇思考组成，话题涉及初学者心态、自我怀疑、习惯、合作与规则。开篇「人人都是创作者」把重新布置房间、解决问题、开展对话也纳入创造的范围；鲁宾将艺术家的生活方式描述为一种注意力实践，强调感知、过滤信息与形成经验之间的联系。
英文原作 The Creative Act: A Way of Being 于 2023 年出版。中文版由重轻翻译，中信出版集团于 2025 年 4 月推出，共 416 页。鲁宾曾与阿黛尔、Jay-Z、Johnny Cash 等音乐人合作，他将音乐制作经验转化为围绕创作过程的思考。
游戏推荐｜《沉星之序》
《时空幻境》《见证者》的制作人 Jonathan Blow 与 Thekla 团队带来新作《沉星之序》。这款叙事解谜冒险游戏包含超过 1000 个手工设计的谜题，玩家将在四个规则各异的平行世界里探索，逐步解锁新的角色与机制。
女王、盗贼、战士、巫师，甚至一艘会说话的小船，都可以成为可操控角色。每个世界有独立的故事、规则和危险；随着角色相遇、世界交汇，原本分开的能力与解谜机制也会相互组合。玩家可以按自己的节奏探索，随时返回不同世界，并通过散落的笔记拼出故事。
游戏由 Arc Games 与 Gamirror Games 发行，已于 10 月 8 日登陆 Steam，支持 Windows PC，提供简体中文界面和字幕。中文配音计划在发售后约一个月更新。截至 10 月 11 日，Steam 总体评价为「好评如潮」。

items.title: Getting old Macromedia Director Games to run on modern Hardware
items.author: speckx
items.summary: When I was a kid in the early 2000s, I spent a lot of time playing games that I borrowed from our local library. Many of them were German point-and-click
items.text:
When I was a kid in the early 2000s, I spent a lot of time playing games that I borrowed from our local library. Many of them were German point-and-click adventure games, since those were the games that ran on my dad’s Windows 95 computer. Even back then, I was interested in tech and always tried to figure out how I could keep playing these games after giving them back to the library, but I, of course, never managed to do it.
A few days ago, I stumbled across one of those failed attempts again: a set of CDs onto which I tried to burn a copy of “Findus bei den Mucklas.” I figured that maybe now was the time where I finally have the skills to do it!

Obviously, the CD I burned back then was unusable, both because CD burners at the time often weren’t able to properly read or write copy-protected CDs and because I haven’t had a computer with a disc drive in the past 10 years.

Thankfully, some helpful soul uploaded a set of full disk images for that and all the other games in the series to

archive.org. It’s not piracy if it’s on there, right?

The game came as a set of three files: a .ccd, a .cue and a .img file. Those are apparently produced by the old

CloneCD program and contain the raw data from the disc, plus additional out-of-band information such as track metadata. Games from that time often came with audio tracks as well, so you could just pop these CDs into a CD player and listen to the soundtrack or other bundled media.

Looking at the .cue file shows that there’s a MODE1 track at the start containing the game files, followed by four AUDIO tracks:

To access the data, I just used the old ccd2iso tool, which failed when it hit the first AUDIO track but was still able to convert the start of the file into a regular ISO that could be mounted.

Mounting the file and trying to copy the data over, I ran into what I believe to be the first copy protection measure:

Some of the files seem to be in the disk image multiple times: once as the real copy and once as a second copy that was either 0 bytes or 256 bytes long and contained random garbage.
My guess is that they did that on purpose to trick some tools into displaying only the fake decoy copy of the file instead of the real one by creating deliberately malformed directory entries on the disk. Windows seems to be able to always read the correct file here (otherwise it wouldn’t work there either of course) but with the different tools I tried, each one of them showed a different combination of files in the end.

Using a combination of PeaZip, Ark, Dolphin and 7z, I ultimately managed to extract the right files from the ISO, but it was mostly manual labour: choosing the files that were the right size and skipping the decoy ones.

At this point, just running the installer seemed easiest, and it surprisingly worked. I ran it using WINEPREFIX=$(pwd)/prefix wine "Installiere Findus4.exe" to make it install into a separate Wine prefix, from which I could copy the installed data afterwards.

Executing Findus4.exe now, of course, didn’t just work, but instead showed a nice error popup saying that the CD was missing.

Simply searching for that message using rg -a "Lege die CD" showed that they just read it from the Pettson3.ini file. They apparently didn’t even bother renaming that file from the previous game.

MESSG=Lege die CD Findus4 ein und versuche es noch einmal.

Searching for a few strings ultimately led to messg being found in Findus4.exe. My first instinct was, of course, to just throw the binary into Ghidra and start looking for it. Surprisingly, the string didn’t show up anywhere using the Search -> For Strings... option, which usually means that the string isn’t actually part of the PE data but some sort of extra payload appended to the end of the executable file.

After some more digging, I found that these games are all Macromedia Director Projector executables. These were generated by Macromedia Director and basically contain the whole runtime for interpreting Director files, with a .dxr file concatenated onto the end. That file is what gets executed when the program runs. It made sense that the CD check would be part of the embedded Director file, because why would the runtime read from a config file called Pettson3.ini?

During my research, I stumbled across

ProjectorRays, which is a disassembler and decompiler for exactly these files. They have the file signature RIFX or XFIR, depending on the endianness of the target system, which makes them pretty easy to identify. Using ImHex, I found a few occurrences of those strings in the binary. Based on the ProjectorRays source code, the format of these .dxr files starts with something like this:

be Content content [[inline]];

else if (magic == "XFIR")

le Content content [[inline]];

std::error("Invalid Director File!");

Only two of the XFIR occurrences had a valid type after them: one was APPL at address 0x00222151, which, according to ScummVM, identifies a Director application wrapper (the executable file we are working with), and the other was MV93 at address 0x002222F0, which seems to be the regular, uncompressed Director movie script.

I initially tried to copy that chunk out of the executable and process it separately using ProjectorRays, but it turned out that all the offsets used inside the appended file are absolute and account for the .dxr file not starting at the beginning of the executable. Instead, I ended up adding an --offset option to the CLI that lets you seek forward to the actual offset of the embedded binary. The PR can be found here in case it’s useful to somebody else:

ProjectorRays#63.

Finally, after all this trouble, we can dump the embedded Director file’s contents using the following command.

./projectorrays decompile Findus4.exe -o output --dump-scripts --offset 0x002222F0

To my surprise, this generated both a disassembly file (the .lasm file) and a decompiled version of the script (the .ls file), which still contains all the original function and variable names!

The generated file is only around 150 lines long and contains the game’s initialization logic. It’s written in a programming language called

Lingo, which is what Macromedia Director uses. Even without knowing the language, it’s pretty straightforward to read. It didn’t take long to find the function from which that "messg" string originally came. As seen here, they implemented a primitive .ini file parser to parse the Pettson3.ini file and get a few config values out of it, one being the error message displayed when no CD can be found.

on analyseIniText iniText

repeat with mening = 1 to iniText.line.count

ReddString = StripString(iniText.line[mening])

if ReddString contains "[" then

ReddString = StripString(iniText.line[mening + 1])

antalBokstaver = ReddString.char.count

if ReddString contains "cdrom" then

cdromenhet = ReddString.char[7..antalBokstaver]

if ReddString contains "Vind" then

antalBokstaver = ReddString.char.count

vindspelAktivt = integer(ReddString.char[6])

if ReddString contains "messg" then

antalBokstaver = ReddString.char.count

alertmessage = ReddString.char[7..antalBokstaver]

if ReddString contains "fullscreen" then

antalBokstaver = ReddString.char.count

fullscreen = integer(ReddString.char[12])

resultat = [#cdromenhet: cdromenhet, #vindspelAktivt: vindspelAktivt, #alertmessage: alertmessage, #screen: fullscreen]

I always find it super fun to read these old scripts and look at the weird mix of broken English, identifiers written in foreign languages (Swedish in this case, I think?) and probably extremely buggy code.

A bit further down, we can also find the function where the error text is actually being used:

seperator = the last char in the applicationPath

drivelista = ["d", "e", "f", "g", "h", "i", "j", "k", "l", "m", "n", "o", "p", "q", "r", "s", "t", "u", "v", "w", "x", "y", "z"]

repeat with Drive in drivelista

iscdrom = baDiskInfo(Drive, "type")

if iscdrom = "CD-ROM" then

Path = Drive & ":" & seperator & "p3media"

-- ... Part of setSearchPaths function

driveletter = checkpccdrompath()

if not voidp(driveletter) then

ini[#cdromenhet] = driveletter & ":"

hdljud = mp & "p3media\p3ljud"

hdcast = mp & "p3media\p3cast"

cdMedia = string(ini.cdromenhet & "\p3media")

cdLjud = string(ini.cdromenhet & "\p3media\p3ljud")

cdCast = string(ini.cdromenhet & "\p3media\p3cast")

the searchPaths = [hdMedia, hdljud, hdcast, cdMedia, cdLjud, cdCast]

alert(string(ini.alertmessage))

Again, pretty straightforward code. They just loop over all possible Windows drives, trying to find one that contains a CD-ROM with the p3media folder on it. If one is found, the search paths are set up. Otherwise, the error message we saw is displayed and the game calls quit().

Analyzing the setSearchPaths function a bit, I figured the easiest way to avoid executing the quit() branch while still allowing it to set up the search paths correctly would be to patch the if to jump to the next instruction instead of the else branch if the check failed. That would result in the CD paths being a bit weird, but I figured it would probably still work, since the game lets you do a “Full Install” where it copies all the required data to the hard disk and presumably loads the files from there.

In the assembly file, the instructions we want to patch are the following:

< 95 00 60 > [246] jmpifz [342] ......... if not voidp(driveletter) then / else

< 4C 08 > [249] getlocal 8 ........... <ini>

ProjectorRays sadly doesn’t yet support assembling the code back, but thankfully, the Lingo bytecode is incredibly simple, so we can do it manually with ImHex. Every instruction starts with a single opcode byte, followed by a big-endian integer that’s either 1, 2 or 4 bytes long. To make the manual patching a bit easier, I also made ProjectorRays output the bytes that make up each instruction (also submitted upstream to ProjectorRays).

Now for the patching: jmpifz has the opcode byte 0x95, followed by the big-endian 16-bit relative offset 0x0060, or 96 bytes, indicating where to jump. To simply jump to the next instruction, we need to jump 3 bytes forward (from offset 246 to offset 249), so we want to patch the instruction bytes to be < 95 00 03 >. Searching for the original byte sequence yielded only a single result at address 0x002252E8, which I overwrote with the new instruction.

And with that, the game’s intro video was playing! 🎉

Sadly, there was more to it.

Again, simply searching for that string yielded two results, and I decided to start with intro.dxr for now.

Throwing it into ProjectorRays again resulted in a few more scripts, one of which was straightforwardly called BehaviorScript 36 - Call Copy-X CD protection DLL (OPTGRAPH.DLL).ls. I didn’t need that much handholding, devs, but thanks either way.

Inside was, as the filename suggested, some code that loads the optgraph.dll located next to the game executable and calls its initdisplay() function. It then checks the return value of that function, and if it doesn’t match some magic value, the game is once again aborted.

if the platform contains "Mac" then

if getReturnVal(me) <> 26079537 then

Interestingly, they didn’t even bother implementing the copy protection for Mac…

To get past this check, we have a few options. We could make the game believe that it’s running on a Mac, patch the comparison against the magic number or patch the DLL to make it always return that constant. Given that the identical check is implemented again in huset.dxr and that I didn’t really want to reverse engineer the runtime and patch the platform detection, I decided to patch optgraph.dll instead.

Opening the DLL in Ghidra showed that it essentially contained only that one function and nothing else.

initdisplay() itself is a bit of a convoluted mess where they send a bunch of low-level commands to the CD drive to somehow construct that magic value from it.

FUN_10001e50(&local_44,0,0x10);

mciSendCommandA(local_c,0x814,0x100);

mciSendCommandA(local_c,0x814,0x102,&local_44);

local_28 = (uint *)(local_40 & 0xff);

local_48 = (char *)(local_40 >> 8 & 0xff);

local_40._0_2_ = local_40._1_2_;

mciSendCommandA(local_c,0x814,0x112,&local_44);

I didn’t spend too much time reversing any of this but instead just used Ghidra’s wonderful Patch Instruction option to replace the first few instructions with a plain and boring MOV and RET.

**************************************************************

**************************************************************

int __stdcall initdisplay(void)

assume FS_OFFSET = 0xffdff000

10001060 b8 31 f1 MOV EAX, 26079537

After struggling for an embarrassingly long time to get Ghidra to properly export the DLL again, I finally managed to do it through File -> Export -> Original File.

This seemed to have been the last thing needed, since the game now gets all the way to the menu screen!

After I was done, I wrote a quick Python script that can apply the patches discussed in this post. This exact script will only work for the German version of the Game that I linked above. However, it shouldn’t be hard to adapt to other versions as well (probably only requires fixing the hash and the offset)

game_dir = Path(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else Path.cwd()

game_dir / "Findus4.exe",

"b33312ff9086c1cbc09d9cde6baa0eff4220a1ed354c9a3211ff6787fff46e39",

bytes.fromhex("95 00 60"),

bytes.fromhex("95 00 03"),

game_dir / "optgraph.dll",

"9897563fd6447976e2780ba0711f6e4e0a5a98a5c5cbecc4cb9bd608d856bd50",

bytes.fromhex("55 8B EC 81 EC F4"),

bytes.fromhex("B8 31 F1 8D 01 C3"),

for path, expected_hash, offset, original, replacement in patches:

data = bytearray(path.read_bytes())

actual_hash = hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()

if actual_hash != expected_hash:

raise SystemExit(f"Unexpected SHA-256 for {path}: {actual_hash}")

if data[offset : offset + len(original)] != original:

raise SystemExit(f"Unexpected bytes at 0x{offset:X} in {path}")

data[offset : offset + len(replacement)] = replacement

verified.append((path, data))

for path, data in verified:

path.chmod(path.stat().st_mode | 0o200)

After spending the evening playing through that game again, I also looked through a few other, similar games that I used to play. It turns out that a surprisingly large number of them used Macromedia and had essentially the same basic copy-protection mechanism. Sadly, there’s no easy way to make a common patch that works for all of these games, but with a little bit of effort, the same process can be applied to them as well.

Being able to play these games again after over 20 years, and maybe even having my future kid play them, makes me really happy :)

I really hope this post can bring the same joy to others as well!

Only two of the XFIR occurrences had a valid type after them: one was APPL at address 0x00222151, which, according to ScummVM, identifies a Director application wrapper (the executable file we are working with), and the other was MV93 at address 0x002222F0, which seems to be the regular, uncompressed Director movie script.

I initially tried to copy that chunk out of the executable and process it separately using ProjectorRays, but it turned out that all the offsets used inside the appended file are absolute and account for the .dxr file not starting at the beginning of the executable. Instead, I ended up adding an --offset option to the CLI that lets you seek forward to the actual offset of the embedded binary. The PR can be found here in case it’s useful to somebody else:
https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=github.com&sz=128
blocks.c: Decompiled Director Script

blocks.x: ProjectorRays#63.
Finally, after all this trouble, we can dump the embedded Director file’s contents using the following command.
./projectorrays decompile Findus4.exe -o output --dump-scripts --offset 0x002222F0
To my surprise, this generated both a disassembly file (the .lasm file) and a decompiled version of the script (the .ls file), which still contains all the original function and variable names!
https://werwolv.net/assets/decompiled_script.DEUGyPJA.png
blocks.c: Decompiled Director Script

blocks.x: The generated file is only around 150 lines long and contains the game’s initialization logic. It’s written in a programming language called
https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=en.wikipedia.org&sz=128
blocks.c: The game's intro video playing

blocks.x: Lingo, which is what Macromedia Director uses. Even without knowing the language, it’s pretty straightforward to read. It didn’t take long to find the function from which that "messg" string originally came. As seen here, they implemented a primitive .ini file parser to parse the Pettson3.ini file and get a few config values out of it, one being the error message displayed when no CD can be found.
on analyseIniText iniText
repeat with mening = 1 to iniText.line.count
ReddString = StripString(iniText.line[mening])
if ReddString contains "[" then
ReddString = StripString(iniText.line[mening + 1])
antalBokstaver = ReddString.char.count
if ReddString contains "cdrom" then
cdromenhet = ReddString.char[7..antalBokstaver]
if ReddString contains "Vind" then
antalBokstaver = ReddString.char.count
vindspelAktivt = integer(ReddString.char[6])
if ReddString contains "messg" then
antalBokstaver = ReddString.char.count
alertmessage = ReddString.char[7..antalBokstaver]
if ReddString contains "fullscreen" then
antalBokstaver = ReddString.char.count
fullscreen = integer(ReddString.char[12])
resultat = [#cdromenhet: cdromenhet, #vindspelAktivt: vindspelAktivt, #alertmessage: alertmessage, #screen: fullscreen]

I always find it super fun to read these old scripts and look at the weird mix of broken English, identifiers written in foreign languages (Swedish in this case, I think?) and probably extremely buggy code.
A bit further down, we can also find the function where the error text is actually being used:
seperator = the last char in the applicationPath
repeat with Drive in drivelista
iscdrom = baDiskInfo(Drive, "type")
if iscdrom = "CD-ROM" then
Path = Drive & ":" & seperator & "p3media"
-- ... Part of setSearchPaths function
driveletter = checkpccdrompath()
if not voidp(driveletter) then
ini[#cdromenhet] = driveletter & ":"
hdljud = mp & "p3media\p3ljud"
hdcast = mp & "p3media\p3cast"
cdMedia = string(ini.cdromenhet & "\p3media")
cdLjud = string(ini.cdromenhet & "\p3media\p3ljud")
cdCast = string(ini.cdromenhet & "\p3media\p3cast")
the searchPaths = [hdMedia, hdljud, hdcast, cdMedia, cdLjud, cdCast]
alert(string(ini.alertmessage))

Again, pretty straightforward code. They just loop over all possible Windows drives, trying to find one that contains a CD-ROM with the p3media folder on it. If one is found, the search paths are set up. Otherwise, the error message we saw is displayed and the game calls quit().

Analyzing the setSearchPaths function a bit, I figured the easiest way to avoid executing the quit() branch while still allowing it to set up the search paths correctly would be to patch the if to jump to the next instruction instead of the else branch if the check failed. That would result in the CD paths being a bit weird, but I figured it would probably still work, since the game lets you do a “Full Install” where it copies all the required data to the hard disk and presumably loads the files from there.
In the assembly file, the instructions we want to patch are the following:
< 95 00 60 > [246] jmpifz [342] ......... if not voidp(driveletter) then / else

ProjectorRays sadly doesn’t yet support assembling the code back, but thankfully, the Lingo bytecode is incredibly simple, so we can do it manually with ImHex. Every instruction starts with a single opcode byte, followed by a big-endian integer that’s either 1, 2 or 4 bytes long. To make the manual patching a bit easier, I also made ProjectorRays output the bytes that make up each instruction (also submitted upstream to ProjectorRays).

Now for the patching: jmpifz has the opcode byte 0x95, followed by the big-endian 16-bit relative offset 0x0060, or 96 bytes, indicating where to jump. To simply jump to the next instruction, we need to jump 3 bytes forward (from offset 246 to offset 249), so we want to patch the instruction bytes to be < 95 00 03 >. Searching for the original byte sequence yielded only a single result at address 0x002252E8, which I overwrote with the new instruction.
And with that, the game’s intro video was playing! 🎉
https://werwolv.net/assets/game_starting.B9PgIx08.png
blocks.c: The game's intro video playing

blocks.x: Sadly, there was more to it.
https://werwolv.net/assets/copy_protection.C1PIXWDL.png
blocks.c: disappointment2.png

blocks.x: Again, simply searching for that string yielded two results, and I decided to start with intro.dxr for now.

Throwing it into ProjectorRays again resulted in a few more scripts, one of which was straightforwardly called BehaviorScript 36 - Call Copy-X CD protection DLL (OPTGRAPH.DLL).ls. I didn’t need that much handholding, devs, but thanks either way.

Inside was, as the filename suggested, some code that loads the optgraph.dll located next to the game executable and calls its initdisplay() function. It then checks the return value of that function, and if it doesn’t match some magic value, the game is once again aborted.
if the platform contains "Mac" then
if getReturnVal(me) <> 26079537 then
Interestingly, they didn’t even bother implementing the copy protection for Mac…

To get past this check, we have a few options. We could make the game believe that it’s running on a Mac, patch the comparison against the magic number or patch the DLL to make it always return that constant. Given that the identical check is implemented again in huset.dxr and that I didn’t really want to reverse engineer the runtime and patch the platform detection, I decided to patch optgraph.dll instead.
Opening the DLL in Ghidra showed that it essentially contained only that one function and nothing else.
initdisplay() itself is a bit of a convoluted mess where they send a bunch of low-level commands to the CD drive to somehow construct that magic value from it.
mciSendCommandA(local_c,0x814,0x100);
mciSendCommandA(local_c,0x814,0x102,&local_44);
local_28 = (uint *)(local_40 & 0xff);
local_48 = (char *)(local_40 >> 8 & 0xff);
mciSendCommandA(local_c,0x814,0x112,&local_44);
I didn’t spend too much time reversing any of this but instead just used Ghidra’s wonderful Patch Instruction option to replace the first few instructions with a plain and boring MOV and RET.
int __stdcall initdisplay(void)
assume FS_OFFSET = 0xffdff000
After struggling for an embarrassingly long time to get Ghidra to properly export the DLL again, I finally managed to do it through File -> Export -> Original File.
This seemed to have been the last thing needed, since the game now gets all the way to the menu screen!
https://werwolv.net/assets/start_menu.BS9j7iUD.png
blocks.c: Start menu screen of the game

blocks.x: After I was done, I wrote a quick Python script that can apply the patches discussed in this post. This exact script will only work for the German version of the Game that I linked above. However, it shouldn’t be hard to adapt to other versions as well (probably only requires fixing the hash and the offset)
game_dir = Path(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else Path.cwd()
game_dir / "Findus4.exe",
"b33312ff9086c1cbc09d9cde6baa0eff4220a1ed354c9a3211ff6787fff46e39",
bytes.fromhex("95 00 60"),
bytes.fromhex("95 00 03"),
game_dir / "optgraph.dll",
bytes.fromhex("55 8B EC 81 EC F4"),
bytes.fromhex("B8 31 F1 8D 01 C3"),
for path, expected_hash, offset, original, replacement in patches:
data = bytearray(path.read_bytes())
actual_hash = hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()
if actual_hash != expected_hash:
raise SystemExit(f"Unexpected SHA-256 for {path}: {actual_hash}")
if data[offset : offset + len(original)] != original:
raise SystemExit(f"Unexpected bytes at 0x{offset:X} in {path}")
data[offset : offset + len(replacement)] = replacement
verified.append((path, data))
for path, data in verified:
path.chmod(path.stat().st_mode | 0o200)

After spending the evening playing through that game again, I also looked through a few other, similar games that I used to play. It turns out that a surprisingly large number of them used Macromedia and had essentially the same basic copy-protection mechanism. Sadly, there’s no easy way to make a common patch that works for all of these games, but with a little bit of effort, the same process can be applied to them as well.
Being able to play these games again after over 20 years, and maybe even having my future kid play them, makes me really happy :)
I really hope this post can bring the same joy to others as well!
Post: Getting old Macromedia Director Games to run on modern Hardware

items.title: Retrofitting language models to operate over bytes
items.author: theanonymousone
items.summary: Recent progress in AI has been driven by end-to-end deep learning systems that learn representations directly from data. Large language models (LLMs) exemplify
items.text:
Recent progress in AI has been driven by end-to-end deep learning systems that learn representations directly from data. Large language models (LLMs) exemplify this trend, achieving strong capabilities by training on massive collections of text3,4. However, despite their apparent generality, contemporary LLMs are not fully end-to-end: before learning can begin, text must first be mapped to a sequence of discrete units called tokens. The choice of tokens, although sometimes overlooked, fundamentally shapes the representations that LLMs learn and the behaviours that they exhibit5,6,7,8,9.

The vast majority of contemporary LLMs use words or parts of words as the tokens in a process known as subword tokenization1,10. This leads to many problems. LLMs that use subword tokenization suffer from limited character-level understanding11,12,13, which especially hinders performance with scientific data, such as code and biological sequences2,14,15,16,17; they are also implicitly biased towards generating particular responses based on how the prompt is tokenized18,19,20, they are restricted in the number of words they can incorporate in their vocabulary, which in practice leads to English-centricity6,21, and they potentially suboptimally allocate their compute2,22. These problems have motivated extensive research into alternatives to subword tokenization, most commonly by using the underlying UTF-8 bytes that the text is encoded as23 as the discrete units. Many earlier byte-level LLMs claim to outperform subword-level LLMs on the efficiency–performance Pareto frontier2,22,24,25,26,27. However, in practice, byte-level LLMs have not seen widespread adoption so far, and all leading LLMs still exclusively rely on subword tokenization.

We hypothesize that the key reason for this mismatch between theory and practice is that existing approaches to byte-level language modelling focus predominantly on training a new byte-level model from a random initialization and comparing it against a subword-level LLM also trained from a random initialization. By contrast, the training of state-of-the-art subword-level LLMs is rapidly evolving, combining innovations in training data curation, model architecture and post-training. Keeping up with this pace is infeasible for byte-level LLM development without extensive investments.

To resolve this mismatch, we introduce a general method for creating byte-level LLMs that achieve performance close to that of state-of-the-art subword-level LLMs across various tasks, while vastly surpassing earlier byte-level LLMs with a comparable parameter count. In contrast to earlier byte-level LLMs that focus predominantly on training from random initialization, we retrofitted an existing subword-level LLM to the byte level using less than 1% of a typical pretraining budget (49.1B tokens in total, where B represents a billion or 109). We refer to this process as byteification. Byteification establishes a connection between existing subword-level LLMs and byte-level LLMs. This let us train the byteified models Bolmo 7B and Bolmo 1B by starting from the existing fully open LLMs Olmo 3 7B28 and OLMo 2 1B29, Bwen 8B by byteifying Qwen3 8B Base30, and Blama 8B by byteifying Llama 3 8B31.

Our architecture first aggregates the byte stream into a sequence of patches, where each patch itself consists of one or more bytes. The patches are then processed by a large transformer32 language model and finally depooled into bytes. Owing to its latent tokenization into byte patches, we refer to this style of architecture as a latent tokenizer language model (LTLM). Examples of LTLMs include the DTP24, BLT22 and H-Net2 models. However, in contrast to earlier work, we specifically designed our architecture to be well suited to byteification (section ‘Byteified language model architecture’). In particular, we resolved a mismatch between the expressivity of subword tokenization and the latent LTLM tokenization. Alongside an efficient two-stage training procedure (section ‘Byteification training procedure’), this allowed us to quickly recover and, in some cases, surpass the performance of the source subword-level LLM. We believe that byteifying provides a key missing research direction by enabling the creation of state-of-the-art byte-level LLMs without extensive investment. This approach is complementary to training from random initialization. Making it cheap to byteify any subword model can quickly unveil high-performing architectures that are promising candidates for training from random initialization as byte-level LLMs.

Our byteified models outperformed, on average, all earlier publicly available byte-level LLMs of comparable size. For example, Bolmo 7B achieved a +16.5% absolute improvement in STEM tasks over BLT 7B, which was trained from random initialization. Bolmo 7B also greatly outperformed the source Olmo 3 on character understanding and was better in certain coding settings. Bwen 8B outperformed Bolmo 7B, exhibiting comparable trends and reaching performance close to and sometimes surpassing the source Qwen model. Furthermore, we found that the byteified models can arbitrarily be further sped up by training with higher ratios of bytes per patch, which is possible only to a limited extent in subword-level LLMs. Finally, we show that existing components in the source LLM ecosystem can be used to adapt a byteified model without any extra training cost; this could further accelerate research on byte-level LLMs.

In aggregate, our results show that byte-level LLMs offer substantial promise as a foundation for future language models, with potential advantages for computational efficiency by reducing energy and deployment costs, for reducing biases introduced by English-centric subword tokenization and for enabling applications that require fine-grained textual understanding, particularly in scientific and technical domains.

Byteified language model architecture

Following the same overall structure as earlier LTLMs (‘Related work’ in Methods), the byteified models can be formalized as shown in Fig. 1. In a nutshell, a local encoder model operating over bytes first creates contextualized byte representations. A neural boundary predictor module then predicts, based on these representations, the byte positions at which to place a boundary. The boundary information is used to derive a sequence of patches: a patch is the contiguous sequence of bytes between consecutive boundaries (including the byte where the end boundary is placed). A pooling module then reduces the contextualized byte representations to a single representation per patch, which is passed through a deep global model. The patch representations contextualized through the global model are depooled back to the byte level and further contextualized through a local decoder model. Finally, the local decoder representations are used to predict the next byte and any other potential information. We chose the local models to be shallow but wide as we found that the embeddings of the original model typically have a high effective rank (Extended Data Fig. 1), and we chose matrix long short-term memory (mLSTM) layers33 to contextualize local information as they retained high performance at high throughput in our experiments (Extended Data Fig. 3). See ‘Byteified model architecture details’ in Methods for a detailed description of the architecture. Our primary departure from earlier architectures lies in the non-causal patch boundary prediction. The boundary predictor of earlier LTLMs uses only the past context to decide on whether to place a boundary (it is causal, referred to as incremental by Pagnoni et al.22). At a glance, this seems necessary: we are aiming to predict the next byte, so we must not leak any information about it. However, although subword-level LLMs use a causality constraint over the subword tokens, the subword tokens themselves do not depend exclusively on past context: subword tokenizers use information about future bytes to place token boundaries. To see this, let us interpret our subword tokenizer as a function that decides whether to place a token boundary after any byte: \({\mathcal{B}}(x):{\{0,1,\ldots ,255\}}^{n}\to {\{0,1\}}^{n}\), where 1 at the nth place denotes a token boundary predicted after the nth byte. Let us assume (1) a vocabulary of English words and subwords, (2) the example text ‘_Hello_Wor!’, which would typically be tokenized as {‘_Hello’, ‘_Wor’, ‘!’}, and (3) the position i = ∣‘_Hello_Wor’∣ − 1 = 9. \({\mathcal{B}}\) (‘_Hello_Wor!’)i = 1, as there is a boundary after ‘r’. However, in the text ‘_Hello_World!’, which would be tokenized as {‘_Hello’, ‘_World’, ‘!’}, we have \({\mathcal{B}}\) (‘_Hello_World!’)i = 0, despite ‘_Hello_Wor!’[:i + 1] = ‘_Hello_World!’[:i + 1] = ‘_Hello_Wor’. In other words, although the subword-level LLM uses only past subword tokens to predict the next subword token, the subword tokens themselves are created by taking future context into account. In this case, this means deciding that ‘_Wor’ should be a token in one case but not in the other, although the text up until that point is equivalent. Current LTLMs, in contrast, cannot take future context into account. This creates a mismatch between the expressivity of LTLM boundary predictors and subword tokenizers. We modified the boundary predictor to resolve this mismatch. In particular, although earlier boundary predictors can be written as

$${\mathcal{B}}{(\hat{e})}_{t}:= \,f({\hat{e}}_{0},{\hat{e}}_{1},\ldots ,{\hat{e}}_{t}),$$

with f a function mapping the byte representations \(\hat{e}\) to boundary scores by using context up to the current byte representation \({\hat{e}}_{t}\) (where t is the index of the current byte), we set our boundary predictor to

$${{\mathcal{B}}}_{\mathrm{byteify}}{(\hat{e})}_{t}:= \,f({\hat{e}}_{0},{\hat{e}}_{1},\ldots ,{\hat{e}}_{t},{\hat{e}}_{t+1}).$$

a, Bolmo architecture: \({\mathcal{T}}\), the tokenization and embedding operation, transforms the input text into one representation per byte. The representations are contextualized with the local encoder \({\mathcal{E}}\) consisting of mLSTM blocks33. The boundary predictor \({\mathcal{B}}\) decides where to place patch boundaries using 1 byte of future context. The representations are then pooled, passed through the global transformer model \({\mathcal{M}}\) and depooled. Finally, the local decoder \({\mathcal{D}}\), which consists of another mLSTM stack, contextualizes the depooled byte representations and the language-modelling head transforms them into next-byte predictions and decides where to place the next patch boundary. b, Subword-level LLMs non-causally set boundaries over the prefill using the external subword tokenizer and then implicitly predict boundaries and the text content during decoding. c, Earlier byte-level LTLMs causally set boundaries with a lightweight boundary predictor during both prefill and decoding. d, Our byteification architecture restores the expressivity of subword-level LLM boundaries by non-causally predicting boundaries for the prefill and then predicting during decoding whether a boundary occurs and the next byte.

That is, we use up to 1 byte of future context. Concretely, we parameterize our boundary predictor as

$${{\mathcal{B}}}_{\mathrm{byteify}}{(\hat{e})}_{t}:= \,\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{{({W}_{q}{\hat{e}}_{t+1})}^{{\rm{T}}}({W}_{k}{\hat{e}}_{t})}{\parallel {W}_{q}{\hat{e}}_{t+1}\parallel \parallel {W}_{k}{\hat{e}}_{t}\parallel }\right)\in [0,1],$$

where Wq and Wk are learned projection matrices as in Hwang et al.2, although we compute the cosine distance between a projection of the representation of the current byte and the byte one position in the future. Even though subword tokenizers in principle have unrestricted access to the future, in practice, we found 1 byte of lookahead largely sufficient to match the behaviour of subword tokenization. As shown in Fig. 1, taking future context into account can also make patches more semantically coherent. For example, in texts containing compounds, such as ‘the flowerbed’, a boundary predictor has three intuitive options: (1) make the entire compound a single patch ‘flowerbed’, (2) place a patch boundary after ‘r’ to create the patch ‘flower’ or (3) place a patch boundary after ‘b’ (once it is evident that this is a compound word) to create ‘flowerb’. Option (2) is arguably the semantically most coherent34; however, for a causal boundary predictor, this would mean having to place a patch boundary after ‘r’ for every text starting with ‘the flower’, including, for example, ‘the flowers’, whereas a non-causal one can adjust based on future context. The byteification strategy of Hwang et al.2 applies supervision based on option (3), that is, predicting the start of the next subword token instead of the end of the previous one, which would create a patch ‘flowerb’, as shown in Fig. 1.

Although using future context is fine for prefilling, we need to know whether to place a boundary without observing the next byte for decoding. We, thus, add a special symbol <b> to the vocabulary and let the local decoder learn to emit <b> at the end of every patch (the local encoder, by contrast, never sees <b>). This is analogous to the output boundary prediction in Fleshman and Van Durme35. In effect, we end up with two boundary predictors: the boundary predictor \({\mathcal{B}}\) ingesting the shallowly contextualized representations from the local encoder with future context (used during prefill) and a boundary predictor as part of the language-modelling head ingesting deeply contextualized representations from the local decoder without future context (used during decoding). Notably, this is precisely equivalent to the behaviour of subword-level LLMs: the prefill is tokenized using the external subword tokenizer (analogous to the boundary predictor \({\mathcal{B}}\)), and output boundaries <b> are implicitly predicted along with the text contents of every subword token upon decoding (analogous to our output boundary predictor), as illustrated in Fig. 1. This lets our byteified model achieve both accurate boundaries and representations faithful to the original model, whereas earlier approaches had to choose either one or the other (Extended Data Table 6). As we are aiming to predict the symbol <b> after every patch, our local decoder becomes a model over \({{\mathbb{R}}}^{n\times d}\to {{\mathbb{R}}}^{(n+k)\times d}\), that is, the local decoder needs to process k more positions. Although this overhead is not prohibitive in principle, it makes it difficult to compare models that use output boundary prediction against models that do not. We, thus, make it effectively zero-cost by doubling our byte vocabulary size from 256 to 512 for every byte by adding a version of the same byte followed by a boundary. Sampling algorithms such as top_p36 then act on the combined vocabulary of size 512. The goal of the local decoder, then, is to predict the current byte and whether it is followed by a boundary at every step. Fusing the boundary symbol turns the local decoder back into an isotropic model. The only remaining overhead is due to the softmax over a set of 512 instead of 256 output tokens, which is negligible.

Byteification keeps the total parameter count close to the parameter count of the source subword-level LLM, as the output embedding matrix is removed but new parameters from the local models are added (‘Byteified model architecture details’ in Methods and Extended Data Table 5).

Byteification training procedure

Our byteifying procedure consists of two stages. In the first stage, we aim to quickly learn weights for the local encoder, local decoder, boundary predictor and language-modelling head. To do so, we introduce a new objective to optimize towards exactly recovering the behaviour of the source subword-level LLM (‘Byteifying procedure’ in Methods). The parameters of the global model stay frozen in this stage. In the second stage, we train the entire model so that it learns to use byte-level information, while also optionally increasing the target compression ratio of bytes per patch. We used a consistent experimental set-up across all experiments (‘Experimental set-up’ in Methods); see Extended Data Table 4 for a full list of training hyperparameter values.

Performance after byteification

We byteified the Qwen3 8B30, Llama 3 8B31 and Olmo 3 7B28 models, and we refer to their byteified variants as Bwen 8B, Blama 8B and Bolmo 7B, respectively. Table 1 compares these models with the source subword-level models as well as with Olmo 3 with continued training on our data mix under the training settings for Bolmo. We additionally compare against existing byte-level LLMs of comparable size: EvaByte 6.5B27, TFree-HAT 7B37 and BLT 7B22. Bwen 8B statistically significantly outperformed all the earlier byte-level models and numerically improved in every category except GenQA (here, it slightly trailed TFree-HAT 7B). Bwen 8B, Blama 8B and Bolmo 7B were also close to matching their respective source models. Bwen 8B outperformed Bolmo 7B due to its more capable backbone. We observed similar trends for the byteified 1B model (Extended Data Table 3) in our 1B evaluation suite (Extended Data Table 2).

Full size table

For the category Code, the byteified models achieved higher pass@16 rates at lower pass@1, indicating that they generated more diverse continuations than the source subword-level models under the given sampling settings, which were equivalent for all models (temperature = 0.6 and top_p = 0.6; Extended Data Table 1). However, concluding that byte-level models are, in fact, better suited to generating more diverse generations would require mapping the quality–diversity Pareto frontier, as the observed increase in diversity could also be explained by differing effects of the sampling settings or engines on byte-level models compared with the original subword-level models. It could be useful to explore this aspect in future work (‘Future directions’ in Supplementary Information).

The byteified models substantially surpassed their subword-level counterpart regarding character understanding. By contrast, the earlier byte-level models did not outperform the subword-level models. This could be explained by character understanding being acquired primarily through scale12, so although byte-level models should require less scale to acquire character understanding, the increased scale of Olmo 3—probably trained on substantially more tokens than the other models—may compensate for this. Bolmo 7B, Bwen 8B and Blama 8B were trained with synthetic data that encouraged character understanding (‘Character-level training data’ in Methods), which sped up the acquisition of this skill. The Olmo 3 model with continued training on our data mix served as a control, having been trained on the same data but with a different architecture. Comparing Olmo 3 7B (CT) and Bolmo 7B, we found that in this setting, the architecture contributed to a slight degradation in the MC, GenQA and Math categories, while leading to substantial degradation in Code (pass@1) and strong improvements in Code (pass@16) as well as character-level understanding.

Increasing model efficiency

A substantial advantage of LTLMs is that—unlike subword-level LLMs—they are not restricted to a fixed, finite set of patches. We next investigated whether we could leverage the increased freedom in our choice of patching strategy to train a faster model by encouraging a higher average number of bytes per patch. In particular, we experimented with ways to change the external boundary supervision from the original subword tokenization boundaries \({{\mathcal{B}}}_{\mathrm{subword}}\) to a subset of those boundaries selected based on byte-pair encoding (BPE)1, next-token entropy or cross-entropy (‘Byteifying procedure’ in Methods).

As the baseline, we increased the number of bytes per patch of the subword-level LLM through tokenizer transfer to SuperBPE tokenizers38. We trained SuperBPE tokenizers on top of the OLMo tokenizer to reach vocabulary sizes of {200k, 400k}, with k representing thousands, using the same 10-GB text sample as ref. 38 for tokenizer training. We used FOCUS39 to initialize the embeddings of the new superword tokens.

Our results are shown in Fig. 2. Through a transfer to SuperBPE, we could speed up the subword-level LLM while retaining performance to a large extent. However, at some vocabulary size threshold, the subword-level LLM becomes Pareto-dominated as the softmax becomes more computationally expensive. For OLMo 2 1B this happens at a vocabulary size between 200k and 400k tokens; although softmax factorizations40,41 would potentially avoid this, they have been observed to lead to slower convergence and increased training instability21 and would require a new embedding initialization methodology. Byte-level LLMs do not suffer from the softmax bottleneck. This would enable an unbounded increase in efficiency for a smooth drop-off in performance.

Results are shown for the source subword-level LLM with tokenizer transfer to SuperBPE and for Bolmo models with the boundary prediction adapted to achieve higher compression (section ‘Increasing model efficiency’). The subword-level LLM becomes Pareto-dominated as the cost of the softmax starts to become more computationally expensive for larger vocabulary sizes. Byte-level LLMs become Pareto-optimal at that point. The shaded region illustrates the optimal performance–efficiency trade-off. Pareto- t and c denote the target compression and the attained compression, respectively. Error bars indicate a 95% confidence interval of the core task macro average from binomial sampling error (n = 53,879 evaluation instances); each point is a single 150,000-step training run.

Interestingly, BPE merges outperformed entropy and cross-entropy merges, in contrast with earlier work using entropy-based patch boundaries22,24. We believe that this may be a pattern specific to the byteifying setting, as the BPE merging strategy makes the fewest distinct merges to achieve any target compression (and thus, in this sense, it is closest to the pretrained model).

Post-training byteified models through task arithmetic

Byteification adds a new component (a byteified model) to the ecosystem around the source LLM. A natural question is: How does this new component interact with the other components of the source LLM ecosystem? We, thus, investigated whether we could merge existing post-trained versions of Olmo 3 to post-train Bolmo without any extra training cost. We used the Olmo 3 checkpoint directly post-trained on following instructions through reinforcement learning (called RL-Zero28) as a case study. We found that we can infuse the instruction-following capabilities from this checkpoint into Bolmo with task arithmetic42 by adding the weight difference between the transformer layers of the post-trained checkpoint and the base Olmo 3 to the corresponding Bolmo layers (Fig. 3).

Although the Bolmo base model originally performed worse than Olmo 3 on IFEval, merging with task arithmetic lifted its performance to on par with the original post-trained checkpoint. We conclude that it is possible to use components of the subword-level LLM ecosystem to improve the corresponding byteified model. This removes the prerequisite for byte-level LLM support in the infrastructure that subword-level LLM post-training has benefitted immensely from43,44 and substantially speeds up iteration times.

A subtle requirement when post-training byteified models through task arithmetic is that the embedding values of the post-trained models need to be resettable to the values of the base model embeddings without a large performance loss, which is generally, but not always, the case (Extended Data Fig. 2).

Benefits of training in two stages

Training in two stages adds implementation complexity. We ran experiments where we immediately started from stage 2 to test whether the extra complexity was warranted. A fair comparison of stage 2 only training with stage 1 + stage 2 training is difficult: stage 1 training required less computation (measured in floating-point operations or FLOPs), as we only backpropagated through a fraction of the global model (‘Byteifying procedure’ in Methods), and was more memory efficient as we needed to store only a small fraction of the optimizer states. We accounted for this difference by approximately matching the FLOPs and disregarding the memory mismatch. Stage 1 needed approximately \(2\times {\mathrm{FLOPs}}_{{\mathcal{M}}}\), whereas stage 2 needed approximately \(3\times {\mathrm{FLOPs}}_{{\mathcal{M}}}\) (×1 for the forward and ×2 for the backward pass through the global model). We, thus, added 9.8B × 2/3 = 6.5B tokens to stage 2 training when omitting stage 1 (increasing the length of stage 2 by 17%). In practice, we believe the factor of 2/3 may have slightly favoured the stage 2 only run as the memory requirements for stage 1 were lower and inference-specific optimizations can be used to speed up the forward pass of the subword-level LLM used in stage 1.

Figure 4 compares the training trajectory of runs with versus without stage 1 training. The 1B model benefitted more from stage 1 training than 7B, indicating that larger models may be more robust to catastrophic forgetting when starting directly with stage 2. The bits-per-byte gap narrowed throughout the training trajectory but remained in favour of adding stage 1. As the absence of stage 1 did not cause a catastrophic degradation, we believe it is a reasonable hypothesis that stage 1 training becomes less important with larger token budgets; however, this might be influenced in non-trivial ways by factors such as the choice of data mix. A key benefit of stage 1 is streamlining experimentation: quickly obtaining a checkpoint that should come close to the performance of the subword-level LLM creates a substantially shorter feedback loop than repeatedly running full training experiments.

Conclusion

We have established byteification as a missing direction for training from random initialization when developing byte-level LLMs. Byteification lets us train byte-level LLMs with a performance close to that of state-of-the-art subword-level LLMs at the 1B and 7B parameter scales. This is enabled by architectural and training decisions specifically designed for byteifying. The byteified models also come close to matching subword-level LLMs in inference speed. We also explored the increased flexibility of the byte-level models, such as arbitrarily decreasing token granularity for faster inference. Byteifying also lets us leverage other components of the ecosystem around the source subword model by byteifying post-trained models in zero-shot mode once the corresponding base model has been byteified. Overall, byteifying could make byte-level LLMs a practical choice with performance close to the level of subword-level LLMs at a small fraction of the resource investment of earlier work. They may enable future research directions for both the byteification setting and training from random initialization of byte-level LLMs (‘Future directions’ in Supplementary Information).

Byteified model architecture details

Our architecture follows the same overall structure as earlier LTLMs, including DTP, BLT and H-Net (‘Related work’ in Methods). It consists of the following components.

Tokenization and embedding

\({\mathcal{T}}\) assigns every input UTF-8 byte in x (we treat x as a sequence over bytes: x ∈ {0, …, 255}n) a corresponding embedding in \({{\mathbb{R}}}^{d}\) from an embedding table containing an entry for every byte. The embedding table over bytes is negligible in size compared with embedding tables over subwords. However, scaling the size and sparsity of the embedding table has been shown to improve performance while having no negative effect on inference speed46. Inspired by the hash embeddings in BLT22,47, we, thus, increased the size of the embedding table. Specifically, we residually added the longest subword embedding (from the original embedding table in the subword-level LLM) that ends at the current byte position to every byte embedding:

$${e}_{i}:= {{\mathcal{T}}}_{\mathrm{Byte}}({x}_{i})+{{\mathcal{T}}}_{\mathrm{SubwordSuffix}}({x}_{:i}),$$

where \({{\mathcal{T}}}_{\mathrm{SubwordSuffix}}\) assigns an embedding to every byte based on the index of the subword token in the vocabulary \({{\mathcal{V}}}_{\mathrm{Subword}}\) with the longest common suffix to the byte sequence up to the current position i. For example, the subword embeddings corresponding to {‘_’, ‘_f’, ‘_fl’, ‘o’, ‘_flow’} could be added to the byte representation of the sequence {‘_’, ‘f’, ‘l’, ‘o’, ‘w’}, assuming none of {‘_flo’, ‘flo’, ‘lo’} are in the original subword vocabulary. Retaining the subword embeddings is not strictly necessary, and we can generally achieve the same perfor

blocks.x: Recent progress in AI has been driven by end-to-end deep learning systems that learn representations directly from data. Large language models (LLMs) exemplify this trend, achieving strong capabilities by training on massive collections of text3,4. However, despite their apparent generality, contemporary LLMs are not fully end-to-end: before learning can begin, text must first be mapped to a sequence of discrete units called tokens. The choice of tokens, although sometimes overlooked, fundamentally shapes the representations that LLMs learn and the behaviours that they exhibit5,6,7,8,9.

The vast majority of contemporary LLMs use words or parts of words as the tokens in a process known as subword tokenization1,10. This leads to many problems. LLMs that use subword tokenization suffer from limited character-level understanding11,12,13, which especially hinders performance with scientific data, such as code and biological sequences2,14,15,16,17; they are also implicitly biased towards generating particular responses based on how the prompt is tokenized18,19,20, they are restricted in the number of words they can incorporate in their vocabulary, which in practice leads to English-centricity6,21, and they potentially suboptimally allocate their compute2,22. These problems have motivated extensive research into alternatives to subword tokenization, most commonly by using the underlying UTF-8 bytes that the text is encoded as23 as the discrete units. Many earlier byte-level LLMs claim to outperform subword-level LLMs on the efficiency–performance Pareto frontier2,22,24,25,26,27. However, in practice, byte-level LLMs have not seen widespread adoption so far, and all leading LLMs still exclusively rely on subword tokenization.

We hypothesize that the key reason for this mismatch between theory and practice is that existing approaches to byte-level language modelling focus predominantly on training a new byte-level model from a random initialization and comparing it against a subword-level LLM also trained from a random initialization. By contrast, the training of state-of-the-art subword-level LLMs is rapidly evolving, combining innovations in training data curation, model architecture and post-training. Keeping up with this pace is infeasible for byte-level LLM development without extensive investments.

To resolve this mismatch, we introduce a general method for creating byte-level LLMs that achieve performance close to that of state-of-the-art subword-level LLMs across various tasks, while vastly surpassing earlier byte-level LLMs with a comparable parameter count. In contrast to earlier byte-level LLMs that focus predominantly on training from random initialization, we retrofitted an existing subword-level LLM to the byte level using less than 1% of a typical pretraining budget (49.1B tokens in total, where B represents a billion or 109). We refer to this process as byteification. Byteification establishes a connection between existing subword-level LLMs and byte-level LLMs. This let us train the byteified models Bolmo 7B and Bolmo 1B by starting from the existing fully open LLMs Olmo 3 7B28 and OLMo 2 1B29, Bwen 8B by byteifying Qwen3 8B Base30, and Blama 8B by byteifying Llama 3 8B31.

Our architecture first aggregates the byte stream into a sequence of patches, where each patch itself consists of one or more bytes. The patches are then processed by a large transformer32 language model and finally depooled into bytes. Owing to its latent tokenization into byte patches, we refer to this style of architecture as a latent tokenizer language model (LTLM). Examples of LTLMs include the DTP24, BLT22 and H-Net2 models. However, in contrast to earlier work, we specifically designed our architecture to be well suited to byteification (section ‘Byteified language model architecture’). In particular, we resolved a mismatch between the expressivity of subword tokenization and the latent LTLM tokenization. Alongside an efficient two-stage training procedure (section ‘Byteification training procedure’), this allowed us to quickly recover and, in some cases, surpass the performance of the source subword-level LLM. We believe that byteifying provides a key missing research direction by enabling the creation of state-of-the-art byte-level LLMs without extensive investment. This approach is complementary to training from random initialization. Making it cheap to byteify any subword model can quickly unveil high-performing architectures that are promising candidates for training from random initialization as byte-level LLMs.

Our byteified models outperformed, on average, all earlier publicly available byte-level LLMs of comparable size. For example, Bolmo 7B achieved a +16.5% absolute improvement in STEM tasks over BLT 7B, which was trained from random initialization. Bolmo 7B also greatly outperformed the source Olmo 3 on character understanding and was better in certain coding settings. Bwen 8B outperformed Bolmo 7B, exhibiting comparable trends and reaching performance close to and sometimes surpassing the source Qwen model. Furthermore, we found that the byteified models can arbitrarily be further sped up by training with higher ratios of bytes per patch, which is possible only to a limited extent in subword-level LLMs. Finally, we show that existing components in the source LLM ecosystem can be used to adapt a byteified model without any extra training cost; this could further accelerate research on byte-level LLMs.

In aggregate, our results show that byte-level LLMs offer substantial promise as a foundation for future language models, with potential advantages for computational efficiency by reducing energy and deployment costs, for reducing biases introduced by English-centric subword tokenization and for enabling applications that require fine-grained textual understanding, particularly in scientific and technical domains.
Byteified language model architecture

Following the same overall structure as earlier LTLMs (‘Related work’ in Methods), the byteified models can be formalized as shown in Fig. 1. In a nutshell, a local encoder model operating over bytes first creates contextualized byte representations. A neural boundary predictor module then predicts, based on these representations, the byte positions at which to place a boundary. The boundary information is used to derive a sequence of patches: a patch is the contiguous sequence of bytes between consecutive boundaries (including the byte where the end boundary is placed). A pooling module then reduces the contextualized byte representations to a single representation per patch, which is passed through a deep global model. The patch representations contextualized through the global model are depooled back to the byte level and further contextualized through a local decoder model. Finally, the local decoder representations are used to predict the next byte and any other potential information. We chose the local models to be shallow but wide as we found that the embeddings of the original model typically have a high effective rank (Extended Data Fig. 1), and we chose matrix long short-term memory (mLSTM) layers33 to contextualize local information as they retained high performance at high throughput in our experiments (Extended Data Fig. 3). See ‘Byteified model architecture details’ in Methods for a detailed description of the architecture. Our primary departure from earlier architectures lies in the non-causal patch boundary prediction. The boundary predictor of earlier LTLMs uses only the past context to decide on whether to place a boundary (it is causal, referred to as incremental by Pagnoni et al.22). At a glance, this seems necessary: we are aiming to predict the next byte, so we must not leak any information about it. However, although subword-level LLMs use a causality constraint over the subword tokens, the subword tokens themselves do not depend exclusively on past context: subword tokenizers use information about future bytes to place token boundaries. To see this, let us interpret our subword tokenizer as a function that decides whether to place a token boundary after any byte: \({\mathcal{B}}(x):{\{0,1,\ldots ,255\}}^{n}\to {\{0,1\}}^{n}\), where 1 at the nth place denotes a token boundary predicted after the nth byte. Let us assume (1) a vocabulary of English words and subwords, (2) the example text ‘_Hello_Wor!’, which would typically be tokenized as {‘_Hello’, ‘_Wor’, ‘!’}, and (3) the position i = ∣‘_Hello_Wor’∣ − 1 = 9. \({\mathcal{B}}\) (‘_Hello_Wor!’)i = 1, as there is a boundary after ‘r’. However, in the text ‘_Hello_World!’, which would be tokenized as {‘_Hello’, ‘_World’, ‘!’}, we have \({\mathcal{B}}\) (‘_Hello_World!’)i = 0, despite ‘_Hello_Wor!’[:i + 1] = ‘_Hello_World!’[:i + 1] = ‘_Hello_Wor’. In other words, although the subword-level LLM uses only past subword tokens to predict the next subword token, the subword tokens themselves are created by taking future context into account. In this case, this means deciding that ‘_Wor’ should be a token in one case but not in the other, although the text up until that point is equivalent. Current LTLMs, in contrast, cannot take future context into account. This creates a mismatch between the expressivity of LTLM boundary predictors and subword tokenizers. We modified the boundary predictor to resolve this mismatch. In particular, although earlier boundary predictors can be written as

with f a function mapping the byte representations \(\hat{e}\) to boundary scores by using context up to the current byte representation \({\hat{e}}_{t}\) (where t is the index of the current byte), we set our boundary predictor to

The representations are contextualized with the local encoder \({\mathcal{E}}\) consisting of mLSTM blocks33. That is, we use up to 1 byte of future context. Concretely, we parameterize our boundary predictor as

$${{\mathcal{B}}}_{\mathrm{byteify}}{(\hat{e})}_{t}:= \,\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{{({W}_{q}{\hat{e}}_{t+1})}^{{\rm{T}}}({W}_{k}{\hat{e}}_{t})}{\parallel {W}_{q}{\hat{e}}_{t+1}\parallel \parallel {W}_{k}{\hat{e}}_{t}\parallel }\right)\in [0,1],$$

where Wq and Wk are learned projection matrices as in Hwang et al.2, although we compute the cosine distance between a projection of the representation of the current byte and the byte one position in the future. Even though subword tokenizers in principle have unrestricted access to the future, in practice, we found 1 byte of lookahead largely sufficient to match the behaviour of subword tokenization. As shown in Fig. 1, taking future context into account can also make patches more semantically coherent. For example, in texts containing compounds, such as ‘the flowerbed’, a boundary predictor has three intuitive options: (1) make the entire compound a single patch ‘flowerbed’, (2) place a patch boundary after ‘r’ to create the patch ‘flower’ or (3) place a patch boundary after ‘b’ (once it is evident that this is a compound word) to create ‘flowerb’. Option (2) is arguably the semantically most coherent34; however, for a causal boundary predictor, this would mean having to place a patch boundary after ‘r’ for every text starting with ‘the flower’, including, for example, ‘the flowers’, whereas a non-causal one can adjust based on future context. The byteification strategy of Hwang et al.2 applies supervision based on option (3), that is, predicting the start of the next subword token instead of the end of the previous one, which would create a patch ‘flowerb’, as shown in Fig. 1.

Although using future context is fine for prefilling, we need to know whether to place a boundary without observing the next byte for decoding. We, thus, add a special symbol <b> to the vocabulary and let the local decoder learn to emit <b> at the end of every patch (the local encoder, by contrast, never sees <b>). This is analogous to the output boundary prediction in Fleshman and Van Durme35. In effect, we end up with two boundary predictors: the boundary predictor \({\mathcal{B}}\) ingesting the shallowly contextualized representations from the local encoder with future context (used during prefill) and a boundary predictor as part of the language-modelling head ingesting deeply contextualized representations from the local decoder without future context (used during decoding). Notably, this is precisely equivalent to the behaviour of subword-level LLMs: the prefill is tokenized using the external subword tokenizer (analogous to the boundary predictor \({\mathcal{B}}\)), and output boundaries <b> are implicitly predicted along with the text contents of every subword token upon decoding (analogous to our output boundary predictor), as illustrated in Fig. 1. This lets our byteified model achieve both accurate boundaries and representations faithful to the original model, whereas earlier approaches had to choose either one or the other (Extended Data Table 6). As we are aiming to predict the symbol <b> after every patch, our local decoder becomes a model over \({{\mathbb{R}}}^{n\times d}\to {{\mathbb{R}}}^{(n+k)\times d}\), that is, the local decoder needs to process k more positions. Although this overhead is not prohibitive in principle, it makes it difficult to compare models that use output boundary prediction against models that do not. We, thus, make it effectively zero-cost by doubling our byte vocabulary size from 256 to 512 for every byte by adding a version of the same byte followed by a boundary. Sampling algorithms such as top_p36 then act on the combined vocabulary of size 512. The goal of the local decoder, then, is to predict the current byte and whether it is followed by a boundary at every step. Fusing the boundary symbol turns the local decoder back into an isotropic model. The only remaining overhead is due to the softmax over a set of 512 instead of 256 output tokens, which is negligible.

Byteification keeps the total parameter count close to the parameter count of the source subword-level LLM, as the output embedding matrix is removed but new parameters from the local models are added (‘Byteified model architecture details’ in Methods and Extended Data Table 5).
Byteification training procedure

Our byteifying procedure consists of two stages. In the first stage, we aim to quickly learn weights for the local encoder, local decoder, boundary predictor and language-modelling head. To do so, we introduce a new objective to optimize towards exactly recovering the behaviour of the source subword-level LLM (‘Byteifying procedure’ in Methods). The parameters of the global model stay frozen in this stage. In the second stage, we train the entire model so that it learns to use byte-level information, while also optionally increasing the target compression ratio of bytes per patch. We used a consistent experimental set-up across all experiments (‘Experimental set-up’ in Methods); see Extended Data Table 4 for a full list of training hyperparameter values.
Performance after byteification

We byteified the Qwen3 8B30, Llama 3 8B31 and Olmo 3 7B28 models, and we refer to their byteified variants as Bwen 8B, Blama 8B and Bolmo 7B, respectively. Table 1 compares these models with the source subword-level models as well as with Olmo 3 with continued training on our data mix under the training settings for Bolmo. We additionally compare against existing byte-level LLMs of comparable size: EvaByte 6.5B27, TFree-HAT 7B37 and BLT 7B22. Bwen 8B statistically significantly outperformed all the earlier byte-level models and numerically improved in every category except GenQA (here, it slightly trailed TFree-HAT 7B). Bwen 8B, Blama 8B and Bolmo 7B were also close to matching their respective source models. Bwen 8B outperformed Bolmo 7B due to its more capable backbone. We observed similar trends for the byteified 1B model (Extended Data Table 3) in our 1B evaluation suite (Extended Data Table 2).
